This page grew out of the software tutorials of a seminar I taught at the
University of Freiburg in the 2024/25 winter term, *Reproducible research
pipelines with R and Quarto*. In it, Master's students in economics took
conflict event data from the raw files to clean data, maps, estimates and a
finished report. What is useful beyond the seminar is kept here, rewritten as a
short start.

It is for former participants who want to look something up, for anyone I have
sent here, and for anyone who has just finished an R course and wants to write
a first report in Quarto. If that is you, skip ahead to [Quarto](#quarto).

## Why work this way {#why}

A reproducible pipeline means that every number, table and figure comes from
code, and that one command rebuilds the whole document from the raw data:

::: {.pipeline}
raw data [→]{.arrow} R code [→]{.arrow} Quarto document [→]{.arrow} web page · Word · PDF · slides
:::

Three habits follow from it:

- **Never edit data by hand.** Keep the raw files as you got them and make
  every change in code.
- **Never copy a result into the text.** Numbers, tables and figures are
  computed where they appear.
- **Keep everything in plain text.** Scripts and Quarto files are text, so
  version control with Git can track every change.

The pay-off comes the second time round: when the data are updated or a
referee asks for another specification, you rerun instead of redo, and text and
results cannot drift apart. Plain text also suits [coding
agents](coding-agents.qmd), which can read, run and change a project like this.

## Set up once {#setup}

1. **Install** [R](https://cloud.r-project.org/), an editor and
   [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/). [RStudio
   Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) is the usual editor and
   comes with Quarto; [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/) is Posit's newer
   one. A separate Quarto install keeps Quarto up to date.

2. **Make one folder per project.** In RStudio, *File › New Project* creates
   the folder and an `.Rproj` file; open the project by double-clicking that
   file. R then starts in the project folder, so every path can be relative to
   it and the project runs on any computer:

   ```
   my-project/
   ├── my-project.Rproj
   ├── data/             raw data, never edited by hand
   ├── report.qmd        text and code
   └── references.bib    bibliography
   ```

   ```r
   births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")    # relative path: works anywhere
   # setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/project")   # works only on your computer
   ```

3. **Start each session clean.** Under *Tools › Global Options › General*,
   untick *Restore .RData into workspace at startup* and set *Save workspace to
   .RData on exit* to *Never*. Restart R now and then (*Session › Restart R*)
   and run your code from the top: if it still works, your results come from
   your code and not from objects left over in memory.

4. **Install a package once, load it in every script.**
   `install.packages("dplyr")` downloads a package, `library(dplyr)` loads it.
   If you need to rerun a project years later, [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html)
   records the package versions it used.

## The R you need first {#r}

The best free introduction is [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/)
[@wickham2023], the seminar's main reference. This section runs one small
pipeline on data that come with R, so you can paste each step into the R
console and get the same result.

### Objects and functions

```{r}
x <- c(2.9, 3.4, 3.1)   # <- assigns; c() combines values into a vector
mean(x)                 # a function applied to x
```

Everything you work with is an object with a name, and you do things to
objects with functions. `?mean` opens the help page of a function.

### Data

```{r}
library(MASS)       # comes with R and contains the data set birthwt
head(birthwt, 3)
```

`birthwt` holds `r nrow(MASS::birthwt)` births at a US hospital in 1986, used
in a textbook on logistic regression [@hosmer1989]: the birth weight in grams
(`bwt`), whether the mother smoked during pregnancy (`smoke`, coded 0 and 1),
her age (`age`), her weight in pounds (`lwt`) and more (see `?birthwt`). Your
own data you read from a file:

```r
dat <- read.csv("data/my-data.csv")              # text file, comma-separated
dat <- readxl::read_excel("data/my-data.xlsx")   # Excel
dat <- haven::read_dta("data/my-data.dta")       # Stata
```

### Clean

```{r}
library(dplyr)

births <- birthwt |>
  mutate(
    smoker    = factor(smoke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    weight_kg = bwt / 1000,
    mother_kg = lwt * 0.4536
  ) |>
  select(weight_kg, smoker, age, mother_kg)

head(births, 3)
```

The pipe `|>` hands the result of one step to the next: take `birthwt`, *then*
add variables with `mutate()`, *then* keep four of them with `select()`.
Turning a 0/1 code into a labelled factor makes every table, figure and model
that follows easier to read.

### Summarise

```{r}
#| label: tbl-means
#| tbl-cap: "Birth weight in kg by whether the mother smoked during pregnancy."
births |>
  group_by(smoker) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight_kg), sd = sd(weight_kg)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

`group_by()` and `summarise()` compute statistics by group, and `knitr::kable()`
formats the result as a table, @tbl-means. For tables ready for a paper, see
[gtsummary](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/), common in medicine, and
[modelsummary](https://modelsummary.com/), common in economics.

### Plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-weight
#| fig-cap: "Birth weight by whether the mother smoked during pregnancy."
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2024)   # the jitter below is random: fix it to get the same figure

ggplot(births, aes(x = smoker, y = weight_kg)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Mother smoked during pregnancy", y = "Birth weight (kg)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A ggplot is built in layers: the data and which variable goes where (`aes()`),
then the geometry (boxes, points), then labels and a theme. In @fig-weight each
birth is a point on top of the boxplot.

### Model

```{r}
fit <- lm(weight_kg ~ smoker + age + mother_kg, data = births)
summary(fit)
```

In these data, babies of mothers who smoked weighed on average
`r round(-1000 * coef(fit)[["smokerYes"]])` g less than babies of mothers of
the same age and weight who did not smoke. That number is not typed into this
page: inline code in the page's source computes it, so it would change with the
data. Whether it is the *effect* of smoking is a question of research design,
not of code; @huntington2021 is a readable introduction to causal inference
with observational data.

## Quarto {#quarto}

Quarto turns a plain-text file that mixes text and code into a finished
document. A `.qmd` file has three parts: a header between two `---` lines,
written in YAML; text, written in Markdown; and code chunks, which run when the
document is rendered. Here is a complete report built from the pipeline above.
Save the two files in one folder and render the first:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# Show the example files as they are, so the page and the files cannot differ
show_file <- function(path) {
  lang <- if (grepl("\\.bib$", path)) "bibtex" else "markdown"
  cat("\n````{.", lang, " filename=\"", basename(path), "\"}\n", sep = "")
  cat(readLines(path), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n````\n\n")
}
show_file("example/report.qmd")
show_file("example/references.bib")
```

### Render

- In RStudio, click *Render* (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K); in Positron, *Preview*.
- In a terminal, `quarto render report.qmd` makes all three formats in the
  header, `quarto render report.qmd --to docx` makes only the Word file, and
  `quarto preview report.qmd` renders again each time you save.

The same file becomes a web page, a Word document and a PDF, each with Table 1,
Figure 1, the numbers in the text, the citation and the list of references in
place.

### What each part does

- **Header.** Title, author, date, the output formats and their options, the
  bibliography. `echo: false` hides the code in the output, which suits a
  report; leave it out for a tutorial like this page.
- **Chunk options.** Lines starting with `#|` set options for one chunk:
  `include: false` runs the chunk but shows nothing, `label` names it, and
  `fig-cap` and `tbl-cap` add captions.
- **Inline code.** `` `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(births)")` `` writes the
  number of births into the sentence; when the data change, the text changes
  with them.
- **Cross-references.** A chunk labelled `fig-…` becomes a numbered figure and
  one labelled `tbl-…` a numbered table; `@fig-weight` in the text becomes
  "Figure 1", with a link in the web page. Equations and sections work the same
  way ([more](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html)).
- **Citations.** `[@hosmer1989]` cites the entry with that key in
  `references.bib`, and the list of references goes at the end. Reference
  managers export `.bib` files; for Zotero, the [Better
  BibTeX](https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/) plugin keeps the file in
  sync. A [citation style](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html)
  such as `csl: apa.csl` sets the format.

### One source, many formats {#formats}

Each of the seminar's four assignments used another format; together they cover
most of what you need:

| Format | In the header | Good for |
|:---------|:--------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Web page | `html` | sharing as a link, or as one file with `embed-resources: true` |
| Word | `docx` | co-authors who edit in Word; `reference-doc` applies your template |
| PDF | `typst`, or `pdf` | papers and theses; `pdf` uses LaTeX, installed once with `quarto install tinytex` |
| Slides | `revealjs` | talks: each `##` heading starts a new slide |

Larger projects are [websites](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/), like this
one, and [books](https://quarto.org/docs/books/), like my [thesis
template](https://github.com/valentinklotzbuecher/ufr_thesis);
[manuscripts](https://quarto.org/docs/manuscripts/) bundle a paper with the
notebooks behind it. When code takes long to run, `freeze` keeps its results
until the code changes ([more](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/code-execution.html)).

## Practise {#practise}

The seminar's assignments make a good path through your own data, or through
one of the data sets that come with R (`data()` lists them):

1. **A web page** with a few of the data steps above and two or three
   references.
2. **A PDF** with a figure and a table, both cross-referenced in the text.
3. **Slides** with an interactive figure or table, made for instance with
   [plotly](https://plotly.com/r/) or [DT](https://rstudio.github.io/DT/).
4. **One source, three outputs**: the same file as web page, PDF and Word.

## Going further {#reading}

The seminar's topics, and where to continue:

- **R and cleaning data:** [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/),
  above all its chapters on tidy data, joins, factors and dates. The [Big Book
  of R](https://www.bigbookofr.com/) lists hundreds of free books on R.
- **Figures:** the [ggplot2 extensions
  gallery](https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/), and Vincent
  Arel-Bundock on [consistent figures in
  Quarto](https://arelbundock.com/posts/quarto_figures/index.html).
- **Maps and georeferenced data:** [Geocomputation with R](https://r.geocompx.org/).
- **Effects and research design:** [The Effect](https://theeffectbook.net/)
  [@huntington2021] and Scott Cunningham's [Causal
  Inference](https://mixtape.scunning.com/); Carlisle Rainey on [equivalence
  tests](https://www.carlislerainey.com/blog/2023-08-18-equivalence-tests/), for
  arguing that an effect is negligible rather than merely not significant.
- **Workflow:** [What They Forgot to Teach You About R](https://rstats.wtf/) on
  projects and paths, [Happy Git and GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/)
  on version control, and Frank Harrell's [R Workflow](https://hbiostat.org/rflow/)
  for reproducible clinical research. LSE's [Data for Data
  Scientists](https://lse-my472.github.io/) is a full course.
- **More Quarto:** Emil Hvitfeldt's [Slidecraft
  101](https://emilhvitfeldt.com/project/slidecraft-101/) on slides, Cameron
  Patrick's [PDF formatting tips for
  theses](https://cameronpatrick.com/post/2023/07/quarto-thesis-formatting/),
  and a [guide to effect sizes and confidence
  intervals](https://matthewbjane.quarto.pub/) written as a Quarto book.
- **Statistics:** Richard McElreath's [Statistical Rethinking
  lectures](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDcUM9US4XdPz-KxHM4XHt7uUVGWWVSus).
- **A thesis topic that matters:** [Effective Thesis](https://www.effectivethesis.org/).

Once this workflow feels familiar, much of the routine can be handed to an AI
agent: see [Coding agents with GitHub](coding-agents.qmd).
